Preface This document summarizes risks to the U.S. Department of War (DOW) mission from the worldwide adoption of advanced energy technologies. Although advanced energy technologies offer many benefits, they also introduce new risks that warrant mitigation. At the request of DOW, the advanced energy technologies included in this document range from batteries/energy storage, photovoltaics, wind, geothermal, synthetic aviation fuels, and hydrogen, to marine/hydrokinetic power. Advanced nuclear energy technologies are discussed only in Appendix F due to the nascent nature of the technology (i.e., lower technology readiness and deployment levels). Risks are projected for the next 10–20 years, and mitigations are identified. Installation and operational energy risks are addressed, but trade-offs, such as when increasing installation energy resilience might increase operational energy risks, are not evaluated. This report does not address the benefits of advanced energy technology adoption and therefore does not consider net gains associated with adopting these technologies, nor does it consider the relative risks of DOW maintaining reliance on legacy energy sources versus advanced energy technologies. This report also does not mention mitigations that are not specifically tied to advanced energy technology risks (e.g., energy efficiency measures). This study did not consider classified material or classified DOW mission areas. China (hereafter referring specifically to the government, not the people) is referenced in this document due to its predominance in advanced energy technology markets, but similar considerations could apply to other nations. Risks are often broken down into three elements: hazards and threats, vulnerabilities, and consequences or impacts. Hazards and threats, often used interchangeably, refer to conditions or events that cause damage, with hazards typically encompassing disruptive events outside human control (e.g., severe winter storms) and threats typically involving human-caused incidents (e.g., cyberattacks). Vulnerabilities are weaknesses in infrastructure, systems, or processes that increase the likelihood and severity of failure when exposed to hazards or threats, which can damage, disrupt, or destroy assets. Impacts can include national security consequences as well as economic and other costs affecting multiple stakeholders (Anderson et al. 2019).
